coordinator_cost.verdict: The reference-patch rule is cheap and it pays for itself twice over, but not the way it was sold. Writing three throwaway solutions cost about 8.5 minutes and 12 frontier turns -- against a worker spend of $0.13 for one usable implementation, that is not obviously a saving. Its real value was diagnostic: the M-2 patch is what surfaced that L-4 supersedes three shipped fixtures, before a single worker token was spent, and the M-5 patch is what caught an anchoring rule that would have broken an assertion the shipped T-3 oracle already made. Both would otherwise have been discovered as a red gate at $0.09 a look.

findings: A reference patch committed at starting_commit is inside the worker's workspace. The first V5-M1 run returned it byte-for-byte. Rule 2 needs the missing clause: the patch lives in the coordinator's working tree, untracked, and is committed only as evidence afterwards. resolve_reference_patch already reads it from repo_root, so nothing in the harness has to change.

The L-2b read-trace false-positives on every Python oracle. parse_strace_reads resolves non-absolute openat paths against the checkout root, but openat(3, "coordinator", ...) is directory-fd-relative -- emitted by shutil.rmtree's fd walk during tempfile.TemporaryDirectory cleanup. V5-M1's oracle was reported as reading three paths that do not exist in the repository. The one-line fix is in hybrid_dispatch.py, a protected path, so all three M-series packets were frozen off-devbox with read_trace: skipped:untraced instead. Rule 2's third field is currently unobtainable for any Python oracle.

The driver's PR step has never worked. gh pr create runs with cwd set to the disposable worktree, which is a clone with no remotes: 'no git remotes found'. Until L-1 landed no run had ever reached a candidate disposition, so the step had never executed. Both V5-M1 dispatches reached candidate with every gate green and every stage exiting 0, and both then failed here. Both PRs were opened by hand from the gate receipt's own diff.

A retry cannot be spent without clearing the worktree by hand: prepare refuses to dispatch two workers into one workspace. L-4's design -- re-run run/gate/receipt, never prepare -- is exactly the fix, which means M-2 is the row that would have unblocked its own retry.

L-4 as specified cannot run end to end even once implemented: the retry packet carries attempt 2, and the mechanical_bulk route in templates/dispatch/hybrid/hybrid-dispatch.v1.json sets max_attempts: 1, so validate_packet would reject every retried stage. That file is protected. The unit oracle is unaffected; the live retry is not.
M-1's gate-red-twice stop fired in production on the second packet it ever saw, on exactly the evidence it was designed to read, and refused the hand-off. The L-2 stop conditions work.

opencode export produced truncated JSON on all three worker sessions ('export was not JSON: Unterminated string'). L-1b records the failure and never fails the step, as designed -- but it means no packet in this series has a usable worker transcript outside the run receipt's worker.stdout.

Rule 1 bounds a packet by outcome, file and oracle. It does not bound the size of the rewrite, and that is the gap V5-M2 fell into: one outcome, one file, one attainable oracle, and an edit shape -- restructure a 400-line function -- that exceeds what this tier can emit in one response. V5-M1 was an additive change of comparable line count and went green first attempt. Additive versus restructuring looks like the real predictor, not size.

D-8's count moves from 1 to 2. V5-M1's clean run is the second green-first-pass with zero escalations attributable to the worker. The void run and both V5-M2 runs are not evidence about the tier: the first measured the coordinator's own patch, and neither M-2 run produced a diff to judge.
